title: Your faith has made you well (Luke 8:40–56)
hookLine: a bleeding woman and a dying girl, twelve years each

cards: Twelve years ties today's two stories together. Jairus, a ruler of the local synagogue, an important man in town, falls at Jesus' feet. His only daughter, about twelve years old, is dying.
Jesus goes, and the crowd presses so tightly it's hard to move. Somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody notices, who has been bleeding for twelve years: as long as Jairus's daughter has been alive.
Luke says she had spent everything she had on doctors, and none could heal her. She doesn't ask for anything. She has a plan.

teach.h: SHE TOUCHED THE BORDER OF HIS GARMENT.
teach.b: Under the law of her time, her bleeding made her ritually unclean, and for twelve years that would have kept her at the edges of worship and of ordinary touch.
She comes up from behind and, in the King James words, "touched the border of his garment: and immediately her issue of blood stanched." She just wants to slip away. But Jesus stops.
"Who touched me?" Peter points out that the whole crowd is pressing against him. But Jesus says, "Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me."
Virtue here means power. Trembling, she comes forward and tells everything in front of everyone.

teach.h: DAUGHTER: THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.
teach.b: And Jesus says: "Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace." Daughter: a family word for a woman kept at the edges, said in public, so the whole town hears she is well.
Made thee whole is the Greek sozo, the same phrase as "thy faith hath saved thee" at Simon's dinner. Healed and saved share one word. But the stop has cost time.
A messenger arrives: "Thy daughter is dead; trouble not the Master."
Jesus says: "Fear not: believe only, and she shall be made whole." At the house, the mourners are wailing.

teach.h: FEAR NOT: BELIEVE ONLY, AND SHE SHALL BE MADE WHOLE.
teach.b: He says she's sleeping, and they laugh at him. He takes her hand: "Maid, arise." She gets up.
And then a very practical line: he tells them to give her something to eat.

how: Some Christians pray with the healing of the woman and Jairus's daughter when they or someone they love is ill, and in some churches prayer for the sick includes a gentle touch on the shoulder or hand.

o: to touch the edge of a holy garment
to heal and to save, in one Greek word
to wake someone gently from sleep

games.q: what's inside Luke 8:40–56 — tap the pairs.
p: touched the border of his garment
and give her something to eat

s: the woman asked Jesus out loud for healing
she touched his garment from behind, hoping no one would notice.
the girl and the woman's illness were both twelve years
a twelve-year-old girl, and twelve years of bleeding.
after raising the girl, Jesus told them to feed her
he commanded to give her meat.

games.q: you're hurrying to a dying girl. someone in the crowd touches your cloak and is healed. what do you do?
o: keep going; the girl can't wait.
stop and ask who touched you, and speak to her.
games.why: Jesus stops, finds her, and calls her daughter in front of everyone. then he still reaches Jairus's house.

practice: Bring to mind two people who need help right now: one loud about it, like Jairus, urgent and asking, and one quiet, like the woman in the crowd, hoping nobody notices.
Notice which one your attention runs to first, then bring the other forward too; in the story, Jesus stops for the woman and still reaches the girl.
If you pray, you can hold both before God together; if you don't, simply keep both in your care.

wordCard.voice: Sozo, the Greek word used for both healing and being saved: Jesus' words to a woman healed after twelve years, said on the way to a twelve-year-old girl he raises with a word, maid, arise.

orig.note: Greek: has saved, has made well. from sozo, used for healing and for salvation.

carryVoice: Your line: only believe. There was room on that road for both of them. See you tomorrow.
